name: Warbler Green
lede: Warbler Green is an olive-yellow, named by Ridgway in 1912 for the dull greenish-yellow plumage common across many warbler species rather than any one bird.

sections.title: A bird-feather olive
sections.body:
Ridgway plated this hue in 1912 at plate IV, hue 23, tone k; Maerz and Paul carried the same first-recorded date of 1912 into their 1930 dictionary, and the ISCC-NBS system later filed it as block 106, a light olive [1]. Warblers are a large, varied family, and many New World warblers share exactly this muted yellow-olive in their backs and wings, which is likely why Ridgway chose the group name rather than a single species [1].

Its nearest look-alikes in our library are [[silver-fern]], almost the same at a distance of 2.8, [[serpentine-green]], a little duller, and [[dusty-hazel-tone]] at a similar distance [2]. The traditional Japanese list carries a related term, *Koke-iro* (苔色), "moss color" [2]. Measured in LCH it is lightness 55, chroma 42 and hue 98 degrees, a fairly saturated yellow-green [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this olive in 505 of 23,781 paintings (2.12%, as photographed), more common than 77% of the named colors we track [3]. It most often plays an accent, in 55% of its 310 strongest matches [3]. Paulus Potter is its most devoted painter, at 4.8 times the baseline rate across his 28 works here, and it is most over-represented in paintings from India, at 2.7 times the expected rate [3]. The earliest dated match runs to 1285, more than six centuries before Ridgway's own 1912 record; the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the pigment was there, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
